rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean, defensible story shapes without pretending company positioning is market proof. Its best move is “For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody, not capability,” which creates a real buyer-protagonist angle instead of another Databricks-centered announcement. B is useful, but “giving the model away to sell everything around it” asserts the monetization story before the facts earn it; that is how a decent strategy memo turns into a pitch a reporter can swat away in six seconds.
gaps_in_A: “For banks and hospitals” is a useful shorthand, but banks and hospitals are examples, not supplied facts; keep them as possible targets, not proof.

“an enterprise that cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API” overstates the update. The facts say Databricks positions this for regulated enterprises, not that all such buyers legally cannot use closed APIs.
“The prevailing belief: proprietary frontier models are the core asset” is a smart analytical frame, but it is not in the supplied facts. It needs to stay framed as a question, not a premise.
gaps_in_B: “to sell everything around it” is invented. The set admits “what the company actually sells around the model (this is not in the facts and must be supplied),” but the headline already treats it as true.
“the model is the loss leader; the data platform, compute, and tooling are the business” is strategy cosplay unless Databricks says it or the writer supplies evidence.
“Is open-source the new enterprise-AI land grab?” is inflated trend language. One Databricks launch does not make a land grab.
B misses A’s cleaner buyer-side custody angle. It has vendor strategy and finance, but less on the regulated customer as the protagonist.
